intro.displayText: Welcome to React, where pages are built from bricks called components! Today you'll make your very first one for the front page of a pet shop.
intro.speechText: Welcome to React, where pages are built from bricks called components! Today you'll make your very first one for the front page of a pet shop.

recap.displayText: Your first React component is on the screen! You can use it just like a tag. Your new word is component, a function that returns what to show.
recap.speechText: Your first React component is on the screen! You can use it just like a tag. Your new word is component, a function that returns what to show.

intro.displayText: React is a library for building user interfaces out of components. You'll learn why the declarative approach helps, how a React project fits together, and how to put one component per file with export and import. Small components with clear names are how big interfaces stay manageable. Then you'll split a game night page into components.
intro.speechText: React is a library for building user interfaces out of components. You'll learn why the declarative approach helps, how a React project fits together, and how to put one component per file with export and import. Small components with clear names are how big interfaces stay manageable. Then you'll split a game night page into components.

recap.displayText: Well done. You split a page into components, each in its own module, and put them together in App. The gotcha: a default export can be imported under any name, so keep the import name matching the component to avoid confusion. Next, we'll look closely at JSX.
recap.speechText: Well done. You split a page into components, each in its own module, and put them together in App. The gotcha: a default export can be imported under any name, so keep the import name matching the component to avoid confusion. Next, we'll look closely at J-S-X.

intro.displayText: JSX is like HTML with superpowers: put curly braces around something, and JavaScript runs right inside your page! Today you'll finish a player card.
intro.speechText: J-S-X is like H-T-M-L with superpowers: put curly braces around something, and JavaScript runs right inside your page! Today you'll finish a player card.

recap.displayText: Superpowers unlocked! You showed variables with curly braces and used `className` instead of `class`. Your new word is JSX, the HTML-like code inside a React component.
recap.speechText: Superpowers unlocked! You showed variables with curly braces and used class name instead of class. Your new word is J-S-X, the H-T-M-L-like code inside a React component.

intro.displayText: JSX looks like HTML, but it compiles to JavaScript. You'll learn how expressions go in curly braces, why attributes use camel case, how inline styles take an object, and when to use fragments. Once you see JSX as JavaScript, its rules stop feeling random. Then you'll build a weather card.
intro.speechText: J-S-X looks like H-T-M-L, but it compiles to JavaScript. You'll learn how expressions go in curly braces, why attributes use camel case, how inline styles take an object, and when to use fragments. Once you see J-S-X as JavaScript, its rules stop feeling random. Then you'll build a weather card.

recap.displayText: Nice work. You calculated values before the return and dropped them into JSX with curly braces. The gotcha: inline styles need an object, so they use double braces and camel case names like font weight. Next, we'll make components reusable with props.
recap.speechText: Nice work. You calculated values before the return and dropped them into J-S-X with curly braces. The gotcha: inline styles need an object, so they use double braces and camel case names like font weight. Next, we'll make components reusable with props.

intro.displayText: What if you want the same component, but with different words on it? Today you'll use props to give pet cards their own names and sounds.
intro.speechText: What if you want the same component, but with different words on it? Today you'll use props to give pet cards their own names and sounds.

recap.displayText: Pet cards galore! You passed props into one component to make lots of different cards. Your new word is props, the information you hand to a component.
recap.speechText: Pet cards galore! You passed props into one component to make lots of different cards. Your new word is props, the information you hand to a component.

intro.displayText: Props are a component's inputs. You'll learn to destructure props, give them default values, pass content with children, and how data flows one way. Reusable components are how teams avoid writing the same card ten times. Then you'll build a product card for a skate shop.
intro.speechText: Props are a component's inputs. You'll learn to destructure props, give them default values, pass content with children, and how data flows one way. Reusable components are how teams avoid writing the same card ten times. Then you'll build a product card for a skate shop.

recap.displayText: Great job. Your product card takes props, has sensible defaults and works for any product. The gotcha: a prop written in quotes is always a string, so numbers like prices need curly braces. Next, we'll render lists with map and keys.
recap.speechText: Great job. Your product card takes props, has sensible defaults and works for any product. The gotcha: a prop written in quotes is always a string, so numbers like prices need curly braces. Next, we'll render lists with map and keys.

intro.displayText: Got a list of snacks? With map, one line of code turns the whole list into items on the page!
intro.speechText: Got a list of snacks? With map, one line of code turns the whole list into items on the page!

recap.displayText: Snack list served! Map turned each snack into a list item. Your new word is key, a name that helps React keep track of each item.
recap.speechText: Snack list served! Map turned each snack into a list item. Your new word is key, a name that helps React keep track of each item.

intro.displayText: Real apps show lists of data. You'll render lists with map, prepare data with filter and reduce, and learn why stable keys matter. Bad keys cause some of the strangest bugs in React apps. Then you'll build a reading tracker from an array of books.
intro.speechText: Real apps show lists of data. You'll render lists with map, prepare data with filter and reduce, and learn why stable keys matter. Bad keys cause some of the strangest bugs in React apps. Then you'll build a reading tracker from an array of books.

recap.displayText: Nicely done. Your tracker renders every book with a stable key and works out its totals from the data. The gotcha: using the array index as a key breaks when items move, so use an I-D. Next, we'll add state.
recap.speechText: Nicely done. Your tracker renders every book with a stable key and works out its totals from the data. The gotcha: using the array index as a key breaks when items move, so use an I-D. Next, we'll add state.

intro.displayText: Right now your components always show the same thing, but state lets them remember and change! Today you'll fix a bakery button that won't count.
intro.speechText: Right now your components always show the same thing, but state lets them remember and change! Today you'll fix a bakery button that won't count.

recap.displayText: The bakery button counts, and that's the end of React Basics! Calling the setter makes React draw the page again. Your new word is state, what a component remembers.
recap.speechText: The bakery button counts, and that's the end of React Basics! Calling the setter makes React draw the page again. Your new word is state, what a component remembers.

intro.displayText: State is data that changes over time and makes React re-render. You'll learn use state, why each render is a snapshot, updater functions, never mutating state, and deriving values instead of storing them. These rules are where most beginner React bugs come from. Then you'll build a scoreboard with a running log of every point.
intro.speechText: State is data that changes over time and makes React re-render. You'll learn use state, why each render is a snapshot, updater functions, never mutating state, and deriving values instead of storing them. These rules are where most beginner React bugs come from. Then you'll build a scoreboard with a running log of every point.

recap.displayText: Well done. Your scoreboard adds to its log without mutating it and works out the leader during render. The gotcha: pushing into a state array changes it without telling React, so make a new array instead. That completes React Basics, and next comes React Apps.
recap.speechText: Well done. Your scoreboard adds to its log without mutating it and works out the leader during render. The gotcha: pushing into a state array changes it without telling React, so make a new array instead. That completes React Basics, and next comes React Apps.
